name: Conventional Barbell Deadlift
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart, bar over mid-foot.
Hinge down and grip the bar just outside your knees.
Brace your core, flatten your back, and drive through the floor to stand up.
Lower the bar back down with control.
coachNote: The deadlift is a hip hinge, not a squat — keep the bar close to your shins the whole way up.
tips: Keep the bar dragging up your shins and thighs.
Brace your core hard before initiating the pull.
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back.
Letting the bar drift away from the body.
benefits: Builds total posterior chain strength.
One of the best exercises for overall strength development.
safetyNotes: Learn the hinge pattern with light weight before loading heavy.
Never round your back under load.
startingPosition: Bar over mid-foot, hips hinged back, flat back.
endingPosition: Standing tall, hips fully extended, shoulders back.

name: Sumo Deadlift
instructions: Stand with a wide stance, toes pointed outward, bar over mid-foot.
Grip the bar inside your knees with a more upright torso than conventional style.
Drive through the floor, pushing your knees out as you stand.
Lower back down with control.
coachNote: Sumo places more emphasis on the hips and less on the lower back compared to conventional deadlifts.
tips: Push your knees out in line with your toes.
Keep your chest more upright than in a conventional pull.
commonMistakes: Knees caving inward during the pull.
Hips rising faster than the chest.
benefits: Reduces lower back demand versus conventional deadlifts.
Strong overload for glutes and adductors.
safetyNotes: Warm up hips and adductors before heavy sets.
Keep the back flat throughout.
startingPosition: Wide stance, bar over mid-foot, upright-ish torso.
endingPosition: Standing tall, hips fully extended.

name: Barbell Romanian Deadlift
instructions: Hold the bar at hip height with a shoulder-width grip.
Push your hips back while keeping a soft knee bend, lowering the bar along your legs.
Stop when you feel a strong hamstring stretch.
Drive your hips forward to return to standing.
coachNote: Unlike a conventional deadlift, this starts from the top — it's a hinge, not a full pull from the floor.
tips: Keep the bar close to your legs throughout.
Stop the descent once your back starts to round.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees too much, turning it into a squat.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom.
benefits: Strong hamstring and glute stretch under load.
Builds hip hinge strength and posterior chain control.
safetyNotes: Only go as low as your hamstring flexibility allows.
Keep the spine neutral throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, bar at hip height.
endingPosition: Hips hinged back, bar around shin height, hamstrings stretched.

name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs.
Hinge at the hips, lowering the dumbbells along your legs with a soft knee bend.
Stop when you feel a hamstring stretch, then drive hips forward to stand back up.
coachNote: A more accessible entry point for learning the hip hinge before progressing to barbell RDLs.
tips: Keep dumbbells close to the legs.
Keep a neutral spine — don't let the lower back round.
commonMistakes: Squatting the movement instead of hinging.
Letting the dumbbells drift away from the legs.
benefits: Beginner-friendly hip hinge pattern.
Independent arm control reduces imbalance.
safetyNotes: Start light while learning the hinge pattern.
Stop the descent before the back rounds.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbells at thigh level.
endingPosition: Hips hinged back, dumbbells around shin height.

name: Rack Pull
instructions: Set the bar on safety pins at about knee height inside a rack.
Grip the bar and set your back flat as in a deadlift.
Drive through the floor to stand up, pulling the bar to full lockout.
Lower the bar back to the pins with control.
coachNote: The shortened range of motion allows heavier loading than a full deadlift, good for building lockout strength.
tips: Keep the same setup discipline as a full deadlift, just from a higher start.
Don't let the reduced range tempt you into sloppy form.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back at the top.
Using momentum to jerk the bar off the pins.
benefits: Builds strong lockout and grip strength.
Allows overload beyond typical deadlift max.
safetyNotes: Set pin height correctly before loading heavy.
Keep the back flat throughout the pull.
startingPosition: Bar on pins at knee height, flat back, gripping the bar.
endingPosition: Standing tall, hips fully extended.

name: Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from the bar with an overhand grip, hands wider than shoulder-width.
Pull your chin above the bar by driving the elbows down.
Lower back down with control to a full hang.
coachNote: One of the best overall back builders — focus on pulling with the elbows, not just the hands.
tips: Initiate the pull by depressing the shoulder blades first.
Avoid excessive kipping/swinging unless training for that specifically.
commonMistakes: Using momentum instead of controlled strength.
Not achieving a full range of motion at the bottom.
benefits: Builds strong lat width and pulling strength.
Requires no equipment beyond a bar.
safetyNotes: Use an assisted pull-up machine or bands if not yet able to do a full rep.
Avoid dropping abruptly from the top.
startingPosition: Full hang, arms extended.
endingPosition: Chin above the bar, elbows bent and pulled down.

name: Chin-Up
instructions: Hang from the bar with an underhand, shoulder-width grip.
Pull your chin above the bar, driving your elbows down and back.
Lower with control back to a full hang.
coachNote: The underhand grip recruits more biceps than a standard pull-up, making it slightly easier for most lifters.
tips: Keep the chest up throughout the pull.
Avoid excessive swinging.
commonMistakes: Only pulling with the arms and neglecting the back.
Partial range of motion.
benefits: Strong lat and biceps builder.
Often more approachable than the standard pull-up for beginners.
safetyNotes: Use assistance (bands/machine) if a full rep isn't possible yet.
Control the descent to protect the elbows.
startingPosition: Full hang, underhand grip.
endingPosition: Chin above the bar.

name: Wide-Grip Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from the bar with a grip noticeably wider than shoulder-width.
Pull up until your chin clears the bar.
Lower with control back to a full hang.
coachNote: The wider grip emphasizes lat width but reduces the range of motion and biceps contribution slightly.
tips: Focus on driving the elbows down and out.
Don't go so wide that shoulder mobility is compromised.
commonMistakes: Grip too wide, limiting range of motion and straining the shoulders.
Excessive kipping.
benefits: Emphasizes lat width.
Good variation to cycle in with standard pull-ups.
safetyNotes: Avoid a grip so wide it causes shoulder discomfort.
Build standard pull-up strength first.
startingPosition: Full hang, wide overhand grip.
endingPosition: Chin above the bar.

name: Neutral-Grip Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from parallel handles with palms facing each other.
Pull up until your chin clears the handles.
Lower with control back to a full hang.
coachNote: The neutral grip is often the most shoulder-friendly pull-up variation.
tips: Keep the elbows tracking close to the body.
Focus on a full stretch at the bottom.
commonMistakes: Partial range of motion.
Excessive body swing.
benefits: Shoulder-friendly grip position.
Good option for lifters with shoulder discomfort in other grips.
safetyNotes: Requires a bar/handle setup with neutral grip attachments.
Control the descent.
startingPosition: Full hang, neutral grip.
endingPosition: Chin above the handles.

name: Assisted Pull-Up (Machine)
instructions: Kneel or stand on the assisted pull-up machine platform, gripping the handles above.
Pull yourself up until your chin clears the handles.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Reduce the assistance weight over time as you get stronger, working toward an unassisted pull-up.
tips: Choose an assistance level that allows 6-10 controlled reps.
Avoid pushing off the platform with your feet.
commonMistakes: Using too much assistance for too long, slowing progress.
Bouncing off the platform.
benefits: Lets beginners build toward a full pull-up safely.
Adjustable difficulty via the assistance stack.
safetyNotes: Step onto and off the platform carefully.
Choose a stable, controlled assistance level.
startingPosition: Kneeling on platform, arms extended, gripping handles.
endingPosition: Chin above the handles.

name: Lat Pulldown (Wide Grip)
instructions: Sit at the lat pulldown machine and grip the bar wider than shoulder-width.
Pull the bar down to your upper chest, driving your elbows down.
Return with control to full arm extension.
coachNote: A great pull-up alternative for beginners since the weight is fully adjustable.
tips: Lean back only slightly, don't use body momentum to pull.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the bottom.
commonMistakes: Leaning back excessively and turning it into a rowing motion.
Pulling the bar behind the neck.
benefits: Adjustable resistance makes it accessible for all levels.
Builds lat width similar to pull-ups.
safetyNotes: Avoid pulling the bar behind the neck.
Keep the movement controlled, not jerky.
startingPosition: Arms extended overhead, gripping the bar.
endingPosition: Bar pulled down to the upper chest.

name: Lat Pulldown (Close Grip)
instructions: Sit at the machine holding a close-grip handle attachment.
Pull the handle down to your upper chest.
Return with control to full arm extension.
coachNote: The close grip increases range of motion slightly and adds more biceps involvement.
tips: Keep your torso upright, minimal leaning.
Squeeze the lats at the bottom of the pull.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to yank the handle down.
Shrugging the shoulders up during the pull.
benefits: Slightly longer range of motion than wide grip.
Good lat and biceps combination exercise.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement smooth and controlled.
Avoid excessive backward lean.
startingPosition: Arms extended overhead, close-grip handle.
endingPosition: Handle pulled to the upper chest.

name: Lat Pulldown (Reverse Grip)
instructions: Sit at the machine gripping the bar with an underhand, shoulder-width grip.
Pull the bar down to your upper chest.
Return with control to full arm extension.
coachNote: Similar to a chin-up in muscle emphasis — strong biceps involvement alongside the lats.
tips: Keep elbows close to the body as you pull.
Avoid leaning back excessively.
commonMistakes: Using the biceps alone instead of driving with the back.
Jerky, momentum-driven reps.
benefits: Strong lat and biceps combination.
Good option for those working toward chin-ups.
safetyNotes: Control the eccentric portion.
Keep wrists neutral.
startingPosition: Arms extended overhead, underhand grip.
endingPosition: Bar pulled to the upper chest.

name: Single-Arm Lat Pulldown
instructions: Attach a single handle to the lat pulldown cable and sit facing the machine.
Pull the handle down to shoulder height on one side, driving the elbow down.
Return with control, then repeat on the other side or complete all reps before switching.
coachNote: Unilateral work like this helps correct imbalances between the left and right lat.
tips: Avoid rotating the torso to assist the pull.
Keep the working shoulder blade depressed throughout.
commonMistakes: Twisting the torso to help pull the handle down.
Using too much weight and losing control.
benefits: Addresses side-to-side strength imbalances.
Allows a fuller stretch and contraction than bilateral pulldowns.
safetyNotes: Brace your core to avoid excessive rotation.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
startingPosition: Arm extended overhead, single handle grip.
endingPosition: Handle pulled down to shoulder height.

name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
instructions: Stand facing a high cable pulley holding a straight bar with arms extended.
Keeping arms straight, pull the bar down to your thighs.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: This isolates the lats without biceps assistance since the elbows stay locked throughout.
tips: Keep a slight forward hip hinge for stability.
Focus on lat squeeze, not arm strength.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows, turning it into a pulldown.
Using the hips to swing the weight down.
benefits: Pure lat isolation without grip or biceps fatigue limiting the set.
Good finisher for back day.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, slightly staggered stance.
Avoid excessive weight that forces elbow bending.
startingPosition: Arms extended overhead holding the bar.
endingPosition: Bar pulled down to the thighs, arms still straight.

name: Barbell Bent-Over Row
instructions: Hinge forward at the hips holding the bar with an overhand grip.
Keep your back flat and pull the bar toward your lower ribs.
Lower the bar back down with control.
coachNote: Keep the torso angle consistent throughout the set — don't stand up gradually as fatigue sets in.
tips: Pull with the elbows, not the hands.
Keep the core braced to protect the lower back.
commonMistakes: Standing up too much and turning it into a shrug.
Rounding the lower back.
benefits: Builds thick, strong back musculature.
Trains the whole posterior chain under tension.
safetyNotes: Keep a flat back throughout the set.
Use a weight that allows strict form.
startingPosition: Hinged forward, bar hanging at arm's length.
endingPosition: Bar pulled to the lower ribs.

name: Pendlay Row
instructions: Set up with the torso parallel to the floor and the bar resting on the ground between reps.
Explosively pull the bar to the lower chest/upper abdomen.
Lower the bar back to a dead stop on the floor before the next rep.
coachNote: Each rep starts from a dead stop on the floor, removing momentum and building strict pulling strength.
tips: Keep the torso angle fixed and parallel to the floor throughout.
Pull explosively but control the descent.
commonMistakes: Torso rising up during the pull.
Using momentum from the hips to heave the bar up.
benefits: Builds strict, momentum-free pulling strength.
Strong back thickness builder.
safetyNotes: Maintain a flat back throughout.
Reset fully between reps rather than bouncing the bar.
startingPosition: Torso parallel to floor, bar on the ground.
endingPosition: Bar pulled to the lower chest.

name: T-Bar Row
instructions: Straddle the T-bar machine or landmine bar with a chest pad or hinged torso.
Grip the handles and pull the weight up toward your torso.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The chest-supported version removes lower back strain, letting you focus purely on pulling.
tips: Drive the elbows back and up, not just up.
Keep shoulder blades retracted at the top of each rep.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to heave the weight up.
Shrugging instead of rowing.
benefits: Builds back thickness effectively.
Chest-supported versions reduce lower back fatigue.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable base throughout the movement.
Avoid jerking the weight with the hips if unsupported.
startingPosition: Arms extended, gripping the handles below the chest.
endingPosition: Handles pulled up toward the torso.

name: Chest-Supported Row (Machine)
instructions: Sit or lie chest-down against the pad and grip the handles.
Pull the handles toward your torso, squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Return with control to full arm extension.
coachNote: The chest support completely removes lower back involvement, ideal for lifters wanting pure back isolation.
tips: Keep the chest pressed into the pad throughout.
Focus on squeezing the shoulder blades, not just bending the elbows.
commonMistakes: Lifting the chest off the pad to use momentum.
Using a grip too wide or narrow to feel the back working.
benefits: Zero lower back strain.
Good option for higher rep, back-focused work.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat/pad height correctly before loading.
Avoid yanking the weight.
startingPosition: Chest against pad, arms extended forward.
endingPosition: Handles pulled to the torso.

name: Seated Cable Row (Wide Grip)
instructions: Sit at the cable row station with feet braced and knees slightly bent.
Grip the wide bar attachment and pull it toward your torso.
Return with control to full arm extension, allowing a stretch.
coachNote: Keep the torso upright and avoid rocking back and forth to move more weight — that shifts work away from the back.
tips: Pull with the elbows, driving them back past the torso.
Keep a slight chest-up posture throughout.
commonMistakes: Excessive torso rocking to add momentum.
Rounding the lower back at the stretch position.
benefits: Adjustable resistance for all levels.
Strong back thickness builder with constant cable tension.
safetyNotes: Keep the lower back neutral, not rounded.
Avoid using the legs to heave the weight.
startingPosition: Arms extended, gripping the bar, slight forward lean.
endingPosition: Bar pulled to the torso, chest up.

name: Seated Cable Row (Close Grip)
instructions: Sit at the cable row station holding a close, neutral-grip handle.
Pull the handle toward your torso, elbows close to your sides.
Return with control to full arm extension.
coachNote: The close, neutral grip tends to hit the mid-back thickness effectively with less shoulder strain.
tips: Keep elbows tucked close to the body.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end range.
commonMistakes: Flaring the elbows out wide.
Using body momentum instead of controlled pulling.
benefits: Strong mid-back thickness builder.
Shoulder-friendly grip angle.
safetyNotes: Keep posture upright throughout.
Avoid jerking the cable.
startingPosition: Arms extended, close-grip handle.
endingPosition: Handle pulled to the torso.

name: Single-Arm Seated Cable Row
instructions: Sit at the cable row station gripping a single handle with one hand.
Pull the handle to your torso, allowing a slight rotation.
Return with control, then repeat on the other side.
coachNote: The slight rotation allowed here can increase the contraction compared to bilateral rows, but keep it controlled.
tips: Brace the core to avoid excessive twisting.
Focus on squeezing the back at full contraction.
commonMistakes: Over-rotating the torso to move more weight.
Using the free hand to brace excessively instead of the core.
benefits: Addresses left-right imbalances.
Allows a fuller range of motion than bilateral rowing.
safetyNotes: Keep rotation controlled and intentional, not excessive.
Maintain a stable seated base.
startingPosition: Arm extended, single handle grip.
endingPosition: Handle pulled to the torso with slight rotation.

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
instructions: Place one knee and hand on a bench for support, holding a dumbbell in the opposite hand.
Pull the dumbbell up toward your hip, driving the elbow back.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A staple unilateral back builder — great for correcting imbalances and building thickness.
tips: Keep the torso roughly parallel to the floor and still throughout.
Pull the elbow back and up, not just up.
commonMistakes: Rotating the torso to help lift the weight.
Using momentum instead of a controlled pull.
benefits: Corrects left-right strength imbalances.
Allows a full stretch and strong contraction.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable base with the supporting knee and hand.
Avoid excessive torso rotation.
startingPosition: Dumbbell hanging at arm's length, torso parallel to floor.
endingPosition: Dumbbell pulled to the hip, elbow bent and back.

name: Two-Arm Dumbbell Row
instructions: Hinge forward holding a dumbbell in each hand, torso roughly parallel to the floor.
Pull both dumbbells up toward your torso.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A good option when a bench isn't available for the single-arm supported version.
tips: Keep the back flat throughout the hinge.
Pull with the elbows, not just the hands.
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back under fatigue.
Standing up gradually as the set progresses.
benefits: Trains both sides simultaneously for efficiency.
Builds back thickness and grip strength together.
safetyNotes: Keep the core braced throughout.
Use a weight that allows a flat back to be maintained.
startingPosition: Hinged forward, dumbbells hanging at arm's length.
endingPosition: Dumbbells pulled to the torso.

name: Kroc Row
instructions: Set up as in a single-arm dumbbell row but with a heavier load and a slightly more upright stance.
Pull the dumbbell explosively toward your hip for high reps.
Lower with control between reps.
coachNote: This is a high-intensity, high-rep row using heavier-than-usual loads — build up to it gradually.
tips: Use lifting straps if grip becomes the limiting factor before the back.
Allow a slight body English but keep it controlled.
commonMistakes: Using so much momentum that the back barely works.
Attempting heavy loads before mastering strict single-arm rows.
benefits: Builds significant back and grip strength.
Effective for pushing past hypertrophy plateaus.
safetyNotes: Master strict single-arm rows before attempting this variation.
Use straps to avoid grip failure limiting a safe rep.
startingPosition: Dumbbell hanging at arm's length, supported stance.
endingPosition: Dumbbell pulled to the hip with some body momentum.

name: Meadows Row
instructions: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment or corner.
Stand alongside it in a staggered stance and grip the sleeve with one hand.
Row the bar up toward your hip, then lower with control.
coachNote: The angled bar path gives a unique stretch and contraction compared to standard dumbbell rows.
tips: Keep the working side hip stable throughout.
Focus on a full stretch at the bottom of each rep.
commonMistakes: Using the legs to help heave the weight instead of the back.
Standing too upright, losing the intended angle.
benefits: Unique loading angle for back development.
Strong unilateral pulling exercise.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end in the landmine attachment.
Start light to learn the bar path.
startingPosition: Staggered stance, gripping the barbell sleeve at the bottom.
endingPosition: Bar pulled up toward the hip.

name: Inverted Row (Bodyweight)
instructions: Set a bar at hip height and lie underneath it, gripping it with both hands.
Keep your body in a straight line and pull your chest to the bar.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A great beginner-friendly row since difficulty is easily adjusted by changing bar height or foot position.
tips: Raise the bar height to make it easier, lower it to make it harder.
Keep the body rigid like a plank throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag.
Partial range of motion.
benefits: Highly scalable difficulty.
No weights required, good for home training.
safetyNotes: Ensure the bar/rack setup is secure before hanging under it.
Keep the core braced to protect the lower back.
startingPosition: Hanging under the bar, arms extended, body straight.
endingPosition: Chest pulled to the bar.

name: Renegade Row
instructions: Start in a plank position gripping a dumbbell in each hand.
Row one dumbbell up to your hip while balancing on the other arm.
Lower it back down and repeat on the other side.
coachNote: This combines a row with an anti-rotation core challenge — keep the hips as still as possible.
tips: Widen your foot stance for more stability.
Avoid rotating the hips as you row.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips twist toward the rowing side.
Using dumbbells too heavy to control balance.
benefits: Trains the back and core stability simultaneously.
Functional, transferable strength pattern.
safetyNotes: Master a standard plank before adding the rowing movement.
Use hex dumbbells for stability if available.
startingPosition: Plank position, hands on dumbbells.
endingPosition: One dumbbell pulled to the hip, balancing on the other arm.

name: Cable Face Pull
instructions: Set a rope attachment at upper chest to head height on the cable machine.
Pull the rope toward your face, separating the ends as you pull.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: Excellent for shoulder health — a great addition to any back or pull day to balance out pressing volume.
tips: Pull with the elbows high, aiming them toward the ceiling.
Squeeze the rear delts and upper back at the end range.
commonMistakes: Pulling too low, turning it into a row.
Using momentum instead of controlled contraction.
benefits: Improves shoulder health and posture.
Strengthens the often-neglected rear delts and upper back.
safetyNotes: Use light-to-moderate weight — this is a technique-focused exercise.
Keep the movement smooth and controlled.
startingPosition: Arms extended forward, gripping the rope ends.
endingPosition: Rope pulled to face level, elbows high and back.

name: Face Pull (Band)
instructions: Anchor a resistance band at face height.
Grip the band with both hands and pull it toward your face, separating your hands.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A convenient warm-up option before pressing or pulling sessions when a cable machine isn't available.
tips: Keep elbows high throughout the pull.
Use a light band — this is about activation, not load.
commonMistakes: Using a band too heavy to control properly.
Pulling with the arms only, not engaging the upper back.
benefits: Portable and equipment-light.
Great shoulder health and warm-up tool.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Ensure the anchor point is secure.
startingPosition: Arms extended forward holding the band.
endingPosition: Band pulled to face level, elbows high.

name: Reverse Pec Deck Fly
instructions: Sit facing the pec deck machine and grip the handles in front of you.
Pull your arms out and back in a wide arc, squeezing the upper back.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A reliable, joint-friendly way to isolate the rear delts and upper back without grip fatigue.
tips: Keep a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
Focus on squeezing the shoulder blades together at the back position.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the arms back.
Cutting the range of motion short.
benefits: Very machine-guided and beginner-friendly.
Effectively isolates the rear delts and upper back.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat height so handles align with shoulder level.
Avoid excessive weight that limits range of motion.
startingPosition: Arms in front of the body, gripping the handles.
endingPosition: Arms extended out to the sides.

name: Rear Delt Dumbbell Fly
instructions: Bend forward at the hips holding a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging down.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides in an arc, squeezing your upper back.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Keep the torso still throughout — the movement comes entirely from the shoulders.
tips: Use a light weight and prioritize the squeeze over load.
Keep a slight bend in the elbows.
commonMistakes: Standing up during the movement, using momentum.
Using too much weight and shortening the range of motion.
benefits: Great rear delt and upper back isolation.
Helps balance out pressing-dominant programs.
safetyNotes: Keep the lower back neutral while bent over.
Choose a light-to-moderate weight.
startingPosition: Bent forward, dumbbells hanging below the shoulders.
endingPosition: Arms raised out to the sides at shoulder height.

name: Barbell Shrug
instructions: Hold the barbell in front of your thighs with an overhand grip.
Elevate your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Keep the movement purely vertical — don't roll the shoulders, which adds no benefit and can strain the joint.
tips: Pause briefly at the top of each rep.
Use lifting straps if grip is the limiting factor.
commonMistakes: Rolling the shoulders instead of a straight up-down motion.
Using momentum from the knees to jerk the weight up.
benefits: Directly targets trap development.
Simple to progressively overload.
safetyNotes: Avoid rolling the shoulders, which can irritate the joint.
Keep the core braced during the lift.
startingPosition: Bar held in front of the thighs, shoulders relaxed.
endingPosition: Shoulders elevated toward the ears.

name: Dumbbell Shrug
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Elevate your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Dumbbells allow a slightly greater range of motion than a barbell for this movement.
tips: Keep arms straight throughout, let the traps do the work.
Pause briefly at the top of each rep.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows to assist the lift.
Using too much weight and shortening the range of motion.
benefits: Simple, effective trap isolation.
Easily done alongside other back or shoulder work.
safetyNotes: Avoid rolling the shoulders.
Keep grip secure — use straps for heavier loads if needed.
startingPosition: Dumbbells at the sides, shoulders relaxed.
endingPosition: Shoulders elevated toward the ears.

name: Trap Bar Shrug
instructions: Stand inside a trap bar gripping the neutral handles at your sides.
Elevate your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The neutral grip of a trap bar is often more comfortable on the wrists than a straight barbell for heavy shrugs.
tips: Keep your torso upright throughout.
Pause briefly at the top for a stronger contraction.
commonMistakes: Rolling the shoulders instead of a straight vertical motion.
Using leg drive to help move the weight.
benefits: Comfortable, neutral grip for heavy loading.
Allows heavier loading than a straight bar for some lifters.
safetyNotes: Keep the core braced throughout the lift.
Avoid jerking the weight up.
startingPosition: Standing inside the trap bar, shoulders relaxed.
endingPosition: Shoulders elevated toward the ears.

name: Cable Shrug
instructions: Stand facing away from a low cable pulley holding a straight or EZ bar attachment.
Elevate your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Cable tension stays constant throughout, unlike free weights which can lose tension at the top.
tips: Keep the movement strictly vertical.
Hold the top position briefly for a stronger contraction.
commonMistakes: Rolling the shoulders.
Leaning forward or back to cheat the weight up.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the range of motion.
Easy to adjust load incrementally.
safetyNotes: Maintain a stable stance throughout.
Avoid using momentum to move the weight.
startingPosition: Standing, arms extended down holding the attachment.
endingPosition: Shoulders elevated toward the ears.

name: Good Morning
instructions: Position a barbell across your upper back as in a squat.
Hinge forward at the hips with a soft knee bend, keeping the back flat.
Return to standing by driving the hips forward.
coachNote: This is a technical exercise — start very light and prioritize a flat back over range of motion.
tips: Keep the bar path close to the body throughout.
Only bend forward as far as your back stays flat.
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back.
Using too much weight before mastering the technique.
benefits: Strengthens the lower back and hamstrings under load.
Builds hip hinge strength that carries over to deadlifts.
safetyNotes: Start with an empty bar or very light load.
Stop immediately if the back begins to round.
startingPosition: Standing, bar across upper back.
endingPosition: Torso hinged forward, back flat, hamstrings stretched.

name: Back Extension (Hyperextension)
instructions: Position yourself on the hyperextension bench with hips at the edge of the pad.
Lower your torso down until you feel a stretch in the hamstrings and lower back.
Raise back up until your body forms a straight line.
coachNote: Avoid hyperextending past a straight line at the top — that adds strain without benefit.
tips: Cross arms over the chest for beginners, hold weight for added resistance.
Move slowly and with control.
commonMistakes: Hyperextending past neutral at the top.
Using momentum to bounce out of the bottom position.
benefits: Strengthens the lower back and posterior chain.
Low equipment demand and beginner-friendly.
safetyNotes: Adjust the pad so hips are positioned correctly.
Don't overextend at the top of the movement.
startingPosition: Torso hinged down over the pad.
endingPosition: Body in a straight line, torso raised.

name: Weighted Back Extension
instructions: Set up on the hyperextension bench as in the bodyweight version, holding a weight plate against your chest.
Lower your torso down until you feel a stretch.
Raise back up until your body forms a straight line.
coachNote: Add load only once bodyweight extensions are easy for 15-20 controlled reps.
tips: Hold the plate close to the chest for balance.
Keep the movement slow and controlled, especially with added weight.
commonMistakes: Adding weight before mastering bodyweight control.
Hyperextending past neutral at the top.
benefits: Progressive overload for lower back strength.
Builds resilience in the posterior chain.
safetyNotes: Start with light added weight.
Stop if you feel any sharp lower back discomfort.
startingPosition: Torso hinged down over the pad, holding a plate.
endingPosition: Body in a straight line, torso raised.

name: Superman
instructions: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended in front of you.
Simultaneously raise your arms, chest, and legs off the floor.
Hold briefly, then lower back down with control.
coachNote: A simple, equipment-free way to activate the lower back and posterior chain before heavier training.
tips: Keep the movement controlled, not a quick bounce.
Squeeze the glutes and lower back at the top.
commonMistakes: Using a quick, bouncing motion instead of a controlled hold.
Overextending the neck upward.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Good warm-up or recovery-day activation exercise.
safetyNotes: Keep the range of motion comfortable — this is not meant to be a maximal extension.
Avoid if experiencing acute lower back pain.
startingPosition: Lying face down, arms extended forward.
endingPosition: Chest, arms, and legs raised off the floor.

name: Bird Dog
instructions: Start on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips.
Extend one arm forward and the opposite leg back simultaneously.
Hold briefly, then return to the starting position and switch sides.
coachNote: A foundational core and lower back stability drill — great for warm-ups or rehab-focused programming.
tips: Keep the hips level throughout, avoid rotating.
Move slowly and with control rather than quickly alternating sides.
commonMistakes: Rotating the hips or shoulders during the extension.
Arching the lower back excessively.
benefits: Builds core and lower back stability.
Low-impact and accessible for all fitness levels.
safetyNotes: Keep the spine neutral throughout.
Move within a comfortable range, don't force extension.
startingPosition: On all fours, spine neutral.
endingPosition: Opposite arm and leg extended in a straight line.

name: Landmine Row
instructions: Straddle a landmine-anchored barbell, hinging forward at the hips.
Grip the sleeve with both hands and row it up toward your torso.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A good option when other rowing equipment is occupied — the converging bar path feels natural for many lifters.
tips: Keep the back flat throughout the hinge.
Pull the elbows back and up.
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back.
Standing up gradually during the set.
benefits: Comfortable, natural bar path for rowing.
Minimal equipment required beyond a barbell and anchor.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end in the landmine attachment or a corner.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Hinged forward, gripping the bar sleeve with both hands.
endingPosition: Bar pulled up toward the torso.

name: Single-Arm Landmine Row
instructions: Straddle a landmine-anchored barbell, hinging forward at the hips.
Grip the sleeve with one hand and row it toward your torso.
Lower with control, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Unilateral loading here helps address side-to-side back imbalances.
tips: Brace the free hand on your knee for support if needed.
Keep the hips square throughout the pull.
commonMistakes: Rotating the torso to help lift the weight.
Rounding the lower back.
benefits: Addresses left-right imbalances.
Comfortable bar path for many lifters.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end firmly.
Keep the core braced throughout the set.
startingPosition: Hinged forward, one hand gripping the bar sleeve.
endingPosition: Bar pulled up toward the torso.

name: Cable Pullover
instructions: Stand facing away from a high cable pulley holding a straight bar or rope with arms extended overhead.
Keeping arms mostly straight, pull the attachment down and back toward your thighs.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: Similar in feel to the straight-arm pulldown, useful for isolating the lats with continuous cable tension.
tips: Keep a slight forward lean for stability.
Focus on the lat stretch and squeeze rather than arm strength.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows too much during the pull.
Using the hips to generate momentum.
benefits: Good lat isolation without grip fatigue limiting the set.
Constant cable tension throughout the range.
safetyNotes: Keep footing stable throughout.
Use a controlled tempo, avoid jerking the weight.
startingPosition: Arms extended overhead, gripping the attachment.
endingPosition: Attachment pulled down toward the thighs.

name: Dumbbell Pullover
instructions: Lie across a bench with only your upper back supported, holding a single dumbbell above your chest.
Lower the dumbbell back and down in an arc behind your head, keeping a slight elbow bend.
Pull it back up over your chest to the starting position.
coachNote: This classic exercise works both the lats and, to a lesser degree, the chest, depending on elbow position.
tips: Keep the elbow bend consistent throughout the movement.
Only lower as far as shoulder mobility comfortably allows.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows more at the bottom, turning it into a triceps-dominant movement.
Lowering too far and straining the shoulders.
benefits: Unique stretch for the lats and rib cage area.
Can be used as an accessory for both chest and back days.
safetyNotes: Use a lighter dumbbell than you'd expect — this is not a heavy-load movement.
Have a spotter hand you the dumbbell into position if needed.
startingPosition: Upper back on bench, dumbbell held above the chest.
endingPosition: Dumbbell lowered behind the head in an arc.

name: Seal Row
instructions: Lie face down on an elevated bench with a barbell positioned underneath.
Grip the bar and pull it up toward the bench.
Lower with control back to a full hang.
coachNote: The chest-supported, face-down setup completely eliminates momentum, making this one of the strictest row variations.
tips: Focus on driving the elbows back rather than just up.
Keep the chest pressed into the bench throughout.
commonMistakes: Using a bench too low, restricting range of motion.
Rushing reps instead of controlling each one strictly.
benefits: Removes all momentum and lower back involvement.
Excellent strict back thickness builder.
safetyNotes: Ensure the bench height allows a full range of motion.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
startingPosition: Face down on bench, arms extended holding the bar.
endingPosition: Bar pulled up to the underside of the bench.

name: Yates Row
instructions: Hinge forward with a more upright torso than a standard bent-over row, gripping the bar with an underhand grip.
Pull the bar up toward your lower abdomen.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The more upright torso and underhand grip allow heavier loading with less lower back strain than a standard bent-over row.
tips: Keep the torso angle consistent throughout the set.
Pull the elbows back and slightly up.
commonMistakes: Standing too upright and turning it into a shrug.
Using excessive momentum to move the weight.
benefits: Allows heavier loading with reduced lower back stress.
Strong biceps and back thickness builder.
safetyNotes: Keep a braced core throughout.
Use a weight that allows strict control.
startingPosition: Hinged forward at roughly 45 degrees, underhand grip.
endingPosition: Bar pulled to the lower abdomen.

name: Machine Row (Chest-Supported, Iso-Lateral)
instructions: Sit or kneel into the machine with chest supported against the pad.
Grip the independent handles and pull them toward your torso, one or both arms at a time.
Return with control to full arm extension.
coachNote: The independent handles let each side move through its own natural path, which some lifters find more comfortable than a fixed bar.
tips: Keep the chest pressed into the pad throughout.
Alternate arms or work both together, depending on your goal.
commonMistakes: Lifting the chest off the pad to add momentum.
Using excessive weight and shortening range of motion.
benefits: Zero lower back strain.
Allows unilateral or bilateral training with the same machine.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat/pad height correctly before loading.
Avoid yanking the handles.
startingPosition: Chest against pad, arms extended forward.
endingPosition: Handles pulled to the torso.

name: Resistance Band Row
instructions: Anchor a resistance band at chest height in front of you.
Grip a handle in each hand and step back to create tension.
Pull the handles toward your torso, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A convenient option for home or travel training when no rowing machine or cables are available.
tips: Step further back to increase resistance.
Keep the chest up and shoulders back throughout.
commonMistakes: Anchor point too high or low, changing the intended angle.
Letting the band snap back uncontrolled.
benefits: Portable, minimal equipment needed.
Adjustable resistance via stance distance or band tension.
safetyNotes: Inspect the band for wear before use.
Ensure the anchor point is secure.
startingPosition: Arms extended forward, band under tension.
endingPosition: Handles pulled to the torso.

name: TRX Row
instructions: Set the TRX straps to a mid-length setting and grip a handle in each hand.
Lean back with arms extended and body in a straight line.
Pull your chest up to your hands.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Difficulty is adjusted by changing your body angle — more upright is easier, more horizontal is harder.
tips: Keep the body rigid like a plank throughout.
Adjust foot position to change difficulty on the fly.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag.
Partial range of motion.
benefits: Highly scalable difficulty via body angle.
Portable, minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Ensure the TRX anchor point is secure before use.
Keep the core braced to protect the lower back.
startingPosition: Leaning back, arms extended, body straight.
endingPosition: Chest pulled up to the hands.
